verdict.rationale: No earnings-call passages were supplied — the "CALL PASSAGES" section arrived empty — so the reasoning below comes solely from the scheme filing and the July 24, 2026 NCLT-convened meeting notice. The transaction is a demerger of the Textile Business Division of Kitex Childrenswear Limited (KCL, the Demerged Company) into Kitex Garments Limited (KGL, the Resulting Company, listed as KITEX), under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(19AA) of the IT Act and the SEBI Scheme Circular. The filing's stated objective is "consolidation of Textile business division of KCL in KGL for better growth so that Kitex Childrenswear Limited can concentrate on its other core activities." The operational trigger given is the existing arrangement in which KCL's textile work was done "as job work with final revenue booked in KGL," while "Considering the huge demand for capacity, KCL has decided to use its full capacity for its own revenue" — i.e. the job-work-into-KGL structure was no longer workable once KCL needed its own capacity. The filing says KCL houses two verticals, Textile Business Division and Remaining Business, whose "nature of risks, returns, growth and competition... are distinct and requires attribution of dissimilar technical and managerial focus"; the textile division employs around 4,900 people and spends on CSR above the statutory limit. The claimed benefits are focused growth, operational efficiencies, business synergies and increased customer focus for textiles; economies of scale and a "common pool of production" by combining similar activities under one entity (KGL being "engaged in the similar business and a pioneer in the said field"); the ability of each business to attract a "different set of investors, strategic partners, lenders and other stakeholders"; insulation and de-risking of the two businesses from one another; and value unlocking through "better price discovery of individual platforms," explicitly to "open-up windows to unlock value through potential divestments and acquisitions." Consideration is new KGL equity shares issued to KCL's shareholders of record on a proportionate basis per the Share Entitlement Ratio, with the undertaking transferring on a going-concern basis at book values, liabilities included. Procedurally, the NCLT Kochi Bench ordered meetings on January 22, 2026 (CA(CAA)/01/KOB/2026), and shareholder and unsecured-creditor meetings were held by video conference on July 24, 2026, with remote e-voting from July 20 to July 23, 2026.

At that meeting no shareholder registered to ask a question, so the Q&A was dispensed with and only a chat box was offered — meaning even the meeting record adds no management commentary on rationale.

verdict.rationale: L&T is not spinning off to shareholders — it is transferring its Realty Undertaking as a going concern to L&T Realty Properties Limited (LTRPL), a wholly-owned subsidiary, by slump sale under a Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013, at an enterprise value of ₹6,300 Cr, with consideration discharged in fully paid-up equity shares of LTRPL issued to L&T, so there is no dilution of shareholding and no change in ownership, voting rights or shareholder interests. Management's stated trigger is that the Realty business has grown in scale and complexity: it has an estimated development potential of approximately 71 million sq ft across Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Bengaluru, NCR and Chennai, achieved pre-sales of approximately ₹10,000 Cr in FY2025-26 (the May 2026 call described this as pre-sales more than doubling to ₹94 billion, aided by launches in Noida and Panvel), yet contributed only about 0.59% of consolidated revenue — a business too big to run as a business unit but too small to be visible inside the parent. The Board's fix is a dedicated platform giving sharper strategic focus, greater operating agility and enhanced managerial accountability, while the business keeps the L&T brand, governance standards and institutional strengths. The structure is also explicitly a capital-raising and partnering vehicle: it is said to provide greater flexibility to access growth capital, attract strategic partners and engage with sector-focused investors, supporting a five-year plan of accelerated pre-sales growth through land acquisitions, joint developments and selective expansion of the commercial portfolio. A second problem solved is group structure: the Jan 2026 and May 2026 calls frame this as the start of a phased consolidation of all group real estate undertakings into one simplified, scalable platform, rather than assets scattered across entities. Management states the reorganisation has no material impact on L&T's engineering, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure businesses, and that employees, customer relationships, ongoing projects, contracts, approvals and licences move across without interruption. It is presented as part of a wider portfolio clean-up — alongside the concession exits, where SPAs were executed to divest 100% of Nabha Power and L&T's entire stake in Hyderabad Metro, both expected to close in Q1 FY27 — aimed at enhancing capital allocation flexibility and improving valuation visibility.
verdict.evolution: The idea surfaces publicly on the Jan 2026 call, where management says the parent has 'initiated' the transfer of the Realty undertaking to LTRPL via slump sale under a Scheme of Arrangement subject to regulatory approvals, and frames it as the start of a phased consolidation of all real estate assets into a unified platform for scale, agility and financial strength. By the May 2026 call the framing has shifted from announcement to execution and justification: the scheme is described as an approved NCLT scheme of arrangement, consolidation of all group real estate undertakings into a single simplified, scalable structure is called the year's primary focus for Realty, and the business's operating momentum is cited as evidence — pre-sales more than doubling to ₹94 billion in FY26 on Noida and Panvel launches — while concession exits (Nabha Power, Hyderabad Metro) run in parallel. The scheme filing then adds the hard terms and the fuller rationale absent from the calls: the ₹6,300 Cr enterprise value, share-based consideration, ~71 million sq ft development potential, the 0.59% revenue contribution, no shareholder dilution, and the capital-access/valuation-visibility arguments. Shareholders approved it at the NCLT-convened meeting of August 4, 2026 (116 members attending) with the requisite majority, following NCLT orders dated June 12, 16 and 25, 2026.

verdict.rationale: Management frames AEL as an incubator whose explicit terminal step is separation: "build, stabilize, scale and unlock" — and they say on the Apr 2026 call that the first three phases are done and "AEL is now getting ready for value unlock through demergers", naming Airports, Roads, the ANIL (new energy) ecosystem and long-term-contracted MDO services as the four independent, sector-leading platforms ready to be separated. The stated reason is maturity of the capex cycle plus a changed earnings mix: core infra and services now contribute 80% of FY26 EBITDA versus 12% when the plan was laid out in 2019 (incubating EBITDA was 60% of H1 FY25, over 70% in H1 FY26), so AEL's consolidated numbers now 'mirror' the group's ~82-85% core-infra profile and the businesses no longer need to sit inside an incubator. The scale cited for Airports specifically: 8 airports, 95.3mn passengers, FY26 income INR13,081 crores (+28%) and EBITDA INR5,394 crores (+55%), 23% of India's passenger traffic and 29% of air cargo, with Navi Mumbai's ~INR20,000 crore regulatory asset base earning a 12-14% return and adding ~INR2,000-3,000 crores EBITDA alone. The problem separation is said to solve is valuation/visibility rather than funding: management says the airport business plan is already "funded", that "does the business need that from its own point of view? We are comfortable with the business plan as it is", but that outside investors are "very much" interested because "it's a premier business of its type in AEL" — i.e. the ask is coming from investors, not lenders or partners. The precondition is operational, not financial: back in Feb 2024 Robbie Singh said AEL would "wait for the demerger of this business until it achieves all these benchmarks" — security/immigration queues, car parking, check-in, and the city-side developments that are meant to make non-aero/non-pax two-thirds of airport EBITDA — flagging the event 3-5 years out. Leverage is managed to make the pieces separable: core infra net external debt ~INR45,000 crores against a ~$4bn regulatory asset base at 3.5-4.5x, versus a deliberately conservative ~$2bn against ~$6bn of operating assets in metals/materials/mining, 3.9x consolidated and expected flat-to-down. Alongside the planned demergers, AEL has already executed the same playbook in cash and paper: the Board approved the demerger of the Food FMCG business into Adani Wilmar with Adani Commodities LLP investments (Aug 2024) because it "has become self-sustained", then exited AWL entirely (13.51% OFS plus the residual 30.42%) for post-tax proceeds of ~INR14,200 crores and total exceptional gains of INR9,215 crores, arguing the swap turns INR250 crores of cash-after-tax from AWL into ~INR5,000 crores — "a 20x improvement" — by redeploying up to INR70,000 crores into core infra at 15-18% returns. The INR24,930 crore rights issue (which also converted ~INR16,000-20,000 crores of promoter shareholder loans into equity) was positioned as balance-sheet preparation "for the next phase of growth", funding airports over the next 12 months plus roads and ANIL.
verdict.evolution: The idea surfaced as a deferral, not a plan: on the Feb 2024 call Robbie Singh said the airport demerger would wait until service benchmarks were met and flagged it "between three to five years from now", and the May 2024 call described AEL as "well poised to develop its incubating portfolio eventually as independent listed verticals in their own right". It then became concrete in reverse order — the Aug 2024 call announced an actual approved demerger of the Food FMCG business into Adani Wilmar, Jan 2025 monetised 13.5% of AWL and quantified the recycling math, and May 2025 began carving Airports out operationally (separate segment reporting and a dedicated airport management team on calls from 30th September 2025). Nov 2025 and Feb 2026 were about preparing the vehicle rather than splitting it — the INR25,000 crore rights issue, shareholder-loan-to-equity conversion, and the EBITDA unlock from Navi Mumbai, Kutch Copper and Ganga Expressway. By Apr 2026 management stated plainly that "value unlock through demergers" is the next phase and named four candidate platforms, with Airports "ready" around FY27-28 and the final decision left to the AEL Board.

points.point: Earliest reference: the Airports demerger is explicitly deferred until passenger-experience and city-side benchmarks are achieved, with the event flagged 3-5 years out (i.e. FY27-29), because the business is being built for 2033-35 (240-250mn pax capacity) and for a 65% non-aero EBITDA mix, not for today.
points.quote: That's why we will wait for the demerger of this business until it achieves all these benchmarks. That's why we flag that event between three to five years from now.

points.point: The incubation model is stated as having separate listing as its endpoint, right after describing 4 of 10 road projects over 70% complete and Ganga Expressway progressing.
points.quote: This leaves Adani Enterprises well poised to develop its incubating portfolio eventually as independent listed verticals in their own right.

points.point: First actual approved separation: the Food FMCG business is demerged into Adani Wilmar together with strategic investments in Adani Commodities LLP, with self-sustainability as the stated test and shareholder value unlock as the stated purpose.
points.quote: In line with this, the Board of Directors of Adani Enterprises have approved the demerger of Food FMCG business of Adani Enterprises to Adani Wilmar, along with its strategic investments in Adani Commodities LLP.

points.point: The separation sequence is implied by the incubation sequence: the declared first-phase focus is airports, green hydrogen, roads and data centre, with services businesses (Digital Labs, Global Capability Center) left unreported until they reach scale "towards the end of this decade".
points.quote: Our focus in the first phase over the next five years is to focus on the incubation of airports, green hydrogen and the roads business plus data center.

points.point: The economics of exiting a matured business are quantified: 13.5% of AWL sold via OFS, post-tax equity proceeds of ~INR14,200 crores enabling up to INR70,000 crores of core-infra investment at 15-18% returns, adding INR11,000 crores of EBITDA and ~INR5,000 crores of cash-after-tax against the INR250 crores of cash-after-tax given up — described as a 20x improvement and "massively accretive".
points.quote: the post-tax equity proceeds of this transaction will be roughly INR 14,200 crores , which will enable Adani Enterprise s to invest up to INR 70,000 crores in its core infra businesses.

points.point: Airports is carved out for reporting purposes because it has become too large to stay buried in AEL: FY25 airport EBITDA INR3,480 crores (+43%, ~INR1,000 crores/quarter run rate, 45% of it Mumbai), heading to INR4,500-5,000 crores, so the airport leadership team begins presenting alongside the CFO and granular segment reporting starts from 30th September.
points.quote: Actually, what we are also planning to do is that because it's now a significantly large part of AEL , meaning it will be closer to the INR 4,500 -5,000 crore s EBITDA in the coming quarters .

points.point: The mix shift that underpins the separation case is quantified, and the INR25,000 crore partly-paid rights issue is positioned as balance-sheet preparation — converting promoter shareholder loans (~INR20,000 crores) into equity and funding airports for the next 12 months plus roads and ANIL.
points.quote: The pleasing part in this result is that the EBITDA from incubating business now contributes over 70%, as against 60% in the comparative last half year.

points.point: "Unlock" is used in the EBITDA sense first: Navi Mumbai (RAB close to INR20,000 crores at a 12-14% WACC-based return), Kutch Copper (INR2,800-3,100 crores EBITDA at 70-80% utilisation) and Ganga Expressway (~INR18,000 crore traffic-risk asset that should double Roads' INR1,500 crore EBITDA) are the assets that must season before the platforms can stand alone; the rights issue closed at INR24,930 crores.
points.quote: In the coming period, first, AEL will unlock EBITDA from Navi Mumbai, Kutch Copper and Ganga Expresswa y. Post stabilization, these 3 assets are expected to add well over INR3,000 crores to EBITDA.

points.point: The clearest statement of intent: demergers are named as the mechanism and four platforms are named as the candidates — Airports, Roads, the ANIL ecosystem and long-term contracted MDO services — on the basis that 80% of FY26 EBITDA now comes from core infrastructure and services.
points.quote: AEL is now getting ready for value unlock through demergers. These businesses are independent, sector -leading , large core infra platform , spread across Airports, Roads, ANIL ecosystem and long -term contract ed MDO services, which are ready to turn into value creation mode.

points.point: The four-phase incubation playbook is spelled out, with AEL positioned as having completed the first three; the EBITDA mix is said to have gone from 12% to 80% core infra since the 2019 plan, mirroring the group's 82-85% core-infra shape.
points.quote: Incubation journey is a repeatable playbook for us: build, stabilize, scale and unlock. We are already past first 3 phases and value unlock is the next phase of our journey.

points.point: Timing and decision rights for the Airports demerger: the business will be operationally ready around FY27-28 and the call then belongs to the AEL Board; Phase 2 of Navi Mumbai (toward 60mn pax) plus city-side development across Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow and Jaipur take ~INR17,000 crores of the INR40,000 crore FY27 capex.
points.quote: I think the airport team -- airport management would be ready by -- they are comfortable around, say, '27, '28. And then -- after that, it's very much for AEL Board to determine.

points.point: Who is asking: separation/outside capital is investor-driven, not required by the business, which management says is already fully funded — so the driver is valuation recognition for a 'premier' asset rather than a financing need.
points.quote: It is just whether our investors interested in that's the question? Yes, very much so because it's a premier business of its type in AEL. But does the business need that from its own point of view? We are comfortable with the business plan as it is for ourselves.

points.point: The balance sheet is run so the pieces can be split cleanly: core infra carries ~INR45,000 crores (just under $5bn) net external debt against a ~$4bn regulatory asset base at a guided 3.5-4.5x, while metals/materials/mining is held deliberately low at ~$2bn against ~$6bn of operating assets given its volatility; consolidated leverage 3.9x, expected flat or slightly down.
points.quote: So we guide to that in the core infra while we are growing, we will be closer to the 3.5 to 4.5 range. And obviously, we'll be lower in relation to the mining.

points.point: Executed separations/reorganisations in the filings: the ACL Scheme moved Adani Cementation and Adani Cement Industries out of AEL into listed Ambuja Cements effective 1st August 2025 for 87,00,000 Ambuja shares and an exceptional gain of INR614.56 crores; the residual 30.42% of AWL was sold, taking FY26 exceptional gains to INR9,215.37 crores and ending AWL's associate status.
points.quote: the Hon'ble NCLT has pronounced the order approving the ACL Scheme, which has become effective from 1st August, 2025 and consequently (a) ACL and a step-down subsidiary Adani Cement Industries Limited cease to be subsidiaries of the Parent Company and (b) the Parent Company has received 87,00,000 equity shares of Ambuja towards consideration and recorded exceptional gain oft 614.56 crores.

points.point: The only scheme actually filed and effected on the AEL side is a tidy-up that consolidates rather than splits: Adani Green Technology Ltd and Adani Emerging Business Pvt Ltd amalgamated into AEL and Adani Tradecom Ltd into Adani New Industries Ltd, NCLT-approved 16th March 2026, effective 1st April 2026, with 90,11,048 AEL shares allotted on 15th April 2026 — i.e. ANIL is being assembled as a single entity, not yet demerged.
points.quote: Consequent upon the Scheme becoming effective:  1. AGTL and AEBPL stands amalgamated with the Company  2. ATL stands amalgamated with ANIL

verdict.what_management_expects: Airports: standalone sector-leading platform, FY26 EBITDA INR5,394 crores (+55%) compounding on a 12-14% regulated return on a rising RAB, plus city-side revenue from FY29-30. ANIL: cash-generating, capacity 2.5x. Roads/MDO: stable long-term contracted cash flows. AEL: an 80%-core-infra incubator recycling exit proceeds (INR14,200 crores from AWL into INR70,000 crores of capex at 15-18%) at 3.5-4.5x leverage, with shareholder value unlocked.
verdict.gaps: No swap ratio, record date, scheme filing, board approval, debt/asset allocation, listing venue or dates for the Airports/Roads/ANIL/MDO demergers; no data-centre or defence treatment; no promoter-stake or tax detail.

verdict.rationale: The supplied material contains no earnings-call passages at all — only a truncated NCLT order (CP(CAA)/55(AHM)2025 in CA(CAA)/41(AHM)2025, lead petitioner JKPL Utility Packaging Solutions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.) — so the reasoning below is the filing's alone, and it is stated entirely in placeholder terms (Transferor Companies 1-4, Transferee Company) with no business names, no financial figures and no identified requesting party. The scheme is a multi-part restructuring rather than a described spin-off: (a) three wholly-owned subsidiaries (Transferors 1-3) amalgamate into the Transferee Company because they are in a 'similar line of business' and the boards decided to consolidate all packaging manufacturing and trading entities under one roof, which is expected to give more efficient use of capital assets, supply chain and customer relationships, flexibility in funding the Transferors' capex, elimination of intra-group transactions and the 'cash flow blockages' they cause, fewer shareholding tiers, fewer duplicated legal and regulatory compliances, and savings on administration of separate entities. (b) Redeemable Preference Shares held by the Transferee in Transferor Company 4 are reduced and converted into an unsecured loan so the investment is reflected 'as a liability' — the filing says this is what 'facilitate[s] the demerger from the Transferor Company 4' under Part D — and that loan is then cancelled automatically when Transferor 4 merges in under Part F; the filing asserts this will not impair Transferor 4's liquidity or ability to meet obligations. (c) After Part E, Transferor Company 4 'would be left with paper and packaging business', and because it and the Transferee are in the same line of business, it too is merged in to consolidate all paper and packaging manufacturing and trading entities, again citing structure rationalisation, fewer compliances and lower administrative cost. (d) Reserves are re-organised by setting off the debit balance of Credit Reserve against the existing credit balance 'in order to right-size the balance sheet' so the books 'present a fair representation of the financial position'. Crucially, the demerged business itself — what leaves Transferor Company 4 under Part E, and why — is not described in the excerpt, so the actual separation rationale is absent from the text provided.
verdict.evolution: No earnings calls were provided, so there is no call-by-call evolution to report and none may be supplied from memory. The only datable sequence in the filing is procedural: Appointed Date 01.04.2024; board approval of the scheme on 13.12.2024; documents filed with BSE and NSE on 30.12.2024; stock-exchange observation letters received 08.08.2025; first-motion application filed 15.08.2025 with order 08.09.2025; creditor/shareholder meetings held 01.11.2025 and 02.11.2025 with chairman's report 10.11.2025; second-motion petition filed 12.11.2025 (e-filed 07.11.2025); notice order 20.11.2025, affidavit of service 11.12.2025; RD representation 12.12.2025 and RoC report 18.11.2025, answered by joint affidavit 17.12.2025. The Regional Director objected that the Appointed Date was ante-dated more than a year before filing contrary to MCA Circular 09/2019, and that assets, liabilities and reserves should transfer at standalone rather than consolidated carrying values.

points.point: Transferors 1-3 are wholly-owned subsidiaries in a similar line of business; the boards decided to consolidate all packaging manufacturing and trading entities under the Transferee Company to use capital assets, supply chain and customer relationships more efficiently.
points.quote: The Transferor Company 1, Transferor Company 2, Transferor Company 3, and the Transferee Company are engaged in similar line of business, and the Board of the respective companies has decided to consolidate all packaging business, manufacturing, and trading entities under the Transferee Company.

points.point: A stated purpose is capex funding flexibility for the three subsidiaries and the removal of intra-group transactions that were trapping cash within the group.
points.quote: Facilitate flexibility in funding the capex of the Transferor Company 1, Transferor Company 2, Transferor Company 3, eliminate intra-group transactions and consequent cash flow blockages which shall result in efficient utilization of capital

points.point: The reduction and conversion of Redeemable Preference Shares into an unsecured loan is explicitly the enabling step for the demerger out of Transferor Company 4, by restating the investment as a liability.
points.quote: The reduction and conversion of Redeemable Preference Shares (RPS) in the manner proposed in the Scheme would enable the Transferee Company to reflect the true nature of investment in the Transferor Company 4 i.e., as a liability, and thereby, facilitate the demerger from the Transferor Company 4 (as a part of the Scheme);

points.point: The converted unsecured loan is cancelled automatically once Transferor Company 4 merges into the Transferee under Part F, with no further instrument required.
points.quote: The RPS issued by Transferor Company 4 (or the Demerged Company) shall, upon the effectiveness of Part D of the Scheme, be converted into an unsecured loan.

points.point: The filing asserts the Part D step leaves Transferor Company 4's liquidity and ability to meet its obligations unaffected.
points.quote: The Scheme would not affect the ability or liquidity of the Transferor Company 4 to meet its obligations/ commitments in the normal course of business upon effectiveness of the Part D of the Scheme.

points.point: After the Part E demerger, Transferor Company 4 retains only the paper and packaging business, which is why it is then merged into the same-line-of-business Transferee Company.
points.quote: Upon effectiveness of Part E of the Scheme, Transferor Company 4 would be left with paper and packaging business and management of Transferor Company 4 and Transferee Company are engaged in the same line of business, and so, the Board of the respective companies have decided to consolidate all paper and packaging business, manufacturing, and trading entities under the Transferee Company;

points.point: Structural simplification is cited for both the amalgamation legs: fewer shareholding tiers and a rationalised corporate structure.
points.quote: Assist in rationalizing the corporate structure and reduction of shareholding tiers.

points.point: Cost and compliance duplication across the separate entities is cited as a problem the consolidation solves.
points.quote: Result in savings of administration and other costs associated with managing separate entities

points.point: The reserve re-organisation sets off the debit balance of Credit Reserve against existing credit balances explicitly to right-size the balance sheet and present a fair view.
points.quote: The Scheme proposes to set off the debit balance of Credit Reserve arising out of effectiveness of the Scheme as on the Appointed Date against the existing credit balance lying under Transferee Company, in order to right-size the balance sheet;

points.point: The regulator challenged the 01.04.2024 Appointed Date as ante-dated more than a year before the 15.08.2025 filing, with no justification in the scheme as MCA Circular 09/2019 requires.
points.quote: In the scheme, no justification has mentioned about gap of more than one year in filing of application and appointed date.

points.point: The petitioners attributed the delay to the listed Transferee's stock-exchange observation process, which took from 30.12.2024 to 08.08.2025.
points.quote: The Transferee Company received the observation letters from the stock exchanges on 08.08.2025.

points.point: The RoC/RD also objected that transfers should be at standalone, not consolidated, carrying values as paras 11.1 and 11.2 provide.
points.quote: In this regard, it is submitted that all the Assets, Liabilities and reserves of the Transferor Companies are required to be transferred at the respective carrying values in the standalone financial statements of the Transferee Company instead of consolidated financial statements.

verdict.what_management_expects: Only group-level effects are stated: consolidation of all packaging, then paper-and-packaging, manufacturing and trading entities under the Transferee Company; more efficient use of capital assets, supply chain and customer relationships; capex funding flexibility; no intra-group cash-flow blockages; fewer shareholding tiers, compliances and administrative costs; and a right-sized balance sheet. Nothing on margins, valuation or per-entity outcomes.
verdict.gaps: No earnings-call passages were supplied; the truncated filing omits the demerger's own rationale, the resulting entities' names and financials, any numbers, and who requested the separation.

verdict.segment_name: Enviro Tech Ventures Limited (Demerged Company; FY2026 shown as Associate "Enviro Tech Ventures Pvt Ltd, formerly named as PSV Agro Products Pvt Ltd" — the Resulting Company)
verdict.measure_notes: No revenue or profit line is disclosed for this business anywhere on these pages. The segment note (Note 39 in all three annual reports) reports only two segments — 'Paper & Packaging' and 'Others' — so Enviro Tech is not a reportable segment and has no segment revenue or segment result (PBIT). The only entity-level figures available are from the consolidation schedule (Note 38f, 'share of Net Assets and Profit/(Loss) of Subsidiaries and Joint Venture'): the amount shown is the group's share of that entity's profit/(loss) after tax as consolidated, which I have put in 'pat'. These are standalone-entity shares in consolidated profit, not segment results, and carry no revenue or operating-profit counterpart. Note also that the FY2024 and FY2025 lines are Enviro Tech Ventures Limited excluding its own subsidiary The Sirpur Paper Mills Limited (listed separately), while the FY2026 line is a differently-constituted entity (the Resulting Company, held as an associate), so the three years are not comparable.

years.source: Annual Report 2024 — page 281
Annual Report 2025 — page 288
Annual Report 2026 — page 271

verdict.not_found: Revenue and operating profit/EBIT/EBITDA for Enviro Tech / PSV Agro in all years; no quarterly figures — the investor presentations supplied carry only history and market-share slides, no financials.

verdict.rationale: The separation at issue is the demerger of the Commercial Vehicles business out of the old Tata Motors Limited into TML Commercial Vehicles Limited, executed together with the amalgamation of the PV subsidiary back into the listed parent, under one Composite Scheme of Arrangement sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai (orders of August 25, 2025 and a rectification order of September 10, 2025), with an appointed date of July 1, 2025 and effective date of October 1, 2025. The Scheme states only two objectives in these texts: to transfer the Commercial Vehicles undertaking to the Resulting Company 'on a going concern basis' in compliance with Section 2(19AA) of the Income-tax Act, and to amalgamate Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited into TML 'with an objective of consolidating the Passenger Vehicles Business with TML', after which TML was renamed Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited and TMLCVL renamed Tata Motors Limited (w.e.f. October 13, 2025). The result is that, as the postal ballot puts it, 'the Commercial Vehicle and Passenger Vehicle businesses of the Company are housed in two separate entities', each with its own reconstituted board and KMP (Shailesh Chandra as MD & CEO of TMPV from October 1, 2025; P B Balaji moved from Group CFO to CEO of Jaguar Land Rover from November 17, 2025), and TMPV left reporting one automotive segment of JLR plus Tata Passenger Vehicles, 'other than CV segment moving out'. Shareholders were handed direct ownership of both: 1 TMLCVL share for every 1 TML share held on the October 14, 2025 record date, with historical cost apportioned 31.15% to the CV entity and 68.85% to TMPV, and the new CV shares listed from November 12, 2025. Management's only economic framing on the calls is accounting and capital: a notional demerger gain of ~Rs. 83,000 Cr (CV business valued at ~Rs. 94,000 Cr by third-party agencies against ~Rs. 11,000 Cr book value of net assets transferred), fully offset by a contra deemed-dividend entry so there is 'absolutely no impact on either distributable reserves or on our net worth'; an India PV business that is net cash (~Rs. 5,000 Cr at Q3 FY26, ~Rs. 7,000 Cr at FY26-end) which 'gives a lot of flex to fund the rich product investment cycle'; and the two entities now declaring dividends separately (Rs. 3 at TMPV plus Rs. 4 at TMLCV, 'a total dividend of Rs. 7 in the year when the demerger was undertaken' versus Rs. 6 before). Costs disclosed are stamp duty: a Rs. 400 Cr provision in Q3 FY26, included within about Rs. 4,100 Cr of FY26 exceptionals. No investor, lender or partner is named anywhere in these texts as having asked for the separation; the only stakeholder input recorded is the shareholder vote, which management described as 'overwhelming votes in our favor', and the nine AGM resolutions passed in July 2026.
verdict.evolution: On the Feb 2025 call (Q3 FY25, January 29, 2025) the demerger was already a filed corporate action awaiting exchange/SEBI NOC, with appointed date July 1 and effective date around October 1, 2025; by the Jun 2025 call (Q4 FY25, May 13, 2025) the shareholder vote had passed overwhelmingly and both dates were reconfirmed, and on the Aug 2025 call (Q1 FY26, August 8, 2025) the NCLT final hearing had concluded that same day with judgment reserved and the October 1 effective date 'on plan'. The Nov 2025 call (Q2 FY26, November 14, 2025) was the first set of results reported post-separation, where management walked through the demerger accounting entries, the Rs. 83,000 Cr notional gain and contra deemed dividend, and the new segment structure. Thereafter the subject narrows to residuals and costs: the Feb 2026 call (February 5, 2026) notes CV is out of the segments and books a Rs. 400 Cr stamp duty provision, and the Jun 2026 call (May 14, 2026) folds stamp duty into FY26 exceptionals and frames the two separate dividends as Rs. 7 combined; the strategic 'why' is never revisited on any of these six calls.

points.point: The Scheme bundles two steps: hiving off the Commercial Vehicles undertaking into TMLCVL on a going concern basis (structured to qualify under Section 2(19AA) of the Income-tax Act), and amalgamating the PV subsidiary into the listed parent — the only explicit objective language in any document supplied.
points.quote: Amalgamation of TMLPV with TML with an objective of consolidating the Passenger Vehicles Business with TML and consequent dissolution of TMLPV without being wound up.

points.point: The November 2025 postal ballot explains the consequence the separation was meant to produce — two self-standing entities — and uses it as the reason to rebuild both boards, appointing Shailesh Chandra MD & CEO of TMPV from October 1, 2025 and P B Balaji as a non-executive director while he became CEO of Jaguar Land Rover from November 17, 2025.
points.quote: In view of the above, it was proposed to reconstitute the Board of Directors of both  the entities .

points.point: Shareholders were given direct ownership of both businesses rather than cash, at a strict 1:1 entitlement on the October 14, 2025 record date, with historical cost of acquisition apportioned 31.15% to the CV entity and 68.85% to TMPV; the CV shares were approved for listing and trading from November 12, 2025.
points.quote: 1 (one) share of the Resulting Company (face value of INR 2/- each fully paid up), for every 1 (one) share of the Demerged Company (face value of INR 2/- each fully paid up) of the same class of shares outstanding and as held by such shareholder in the Demerged Company, without any further application, act or deed (‘Share Entitlement Ratio’).

points.point: At the 81st AGM (July 8, 2026) the Chairman and the MD & CEO presented the demerger as completed and as the platform for TMPV's own roadmap, pairing it with JLR's new Panapakkam, Tamil Nadu production and with long-term growth aspirations to FY31 on a consolidated basis.
points.quote: He highlighted the demerger of Commercial Vehicles business into a separate legal entity and commencement of commercial production by JLR at Panapakkam, Tamil Nadu reflecting the synergy between the Company and JLR.

points.point: The demerger was presented purely as a corporate action on track — filings with the exchanges and SEBI complete, operational carve-out work advanced, appointed date July 1 and effective date around October 1, 2025 — alongside the parallel Tata Motors Finance merger into Tata Capital.
points.quote: Operational activities are in an advanced stage and progressing as per plan.

points.point: Management reported that shareholders had backed the Scheme decisively and that both the appointed and effective dates were intact; asked about asset allocation, Balaji confirmed the Tata Capital stake would sit with the CV business after separation.
points.quote: we had overwhelming votes in our favor and therefore we are on track for an appointed date of July 1st

points.point: The NCLT final hearing concluded on the day of the call with judgment reserved, which management said would let them complete the demerger within the quarter for an October 1 effective date; the same slide carried the CV side's Iveco acquisition, i.e. each business already pursuing its own agenda.
points.quote: Hot of the press is the demerger.

points.point: First results after separation: the demerger produced a ~Rs. 83,000 Cr book gain on disposal of the CV undertaking (CV valued at ~Rs. 94,000 Cr by third-party agencies versus ~Rs. 11,000 Cr book value of net assets transferred), but it is entirely notional with no effect on net worth or distributable reserves.
points.quote: But this is only a notional gain as there is a contra entry of ~Rs. 83,000 Cr as a deemed dividend.

points.point: Reporting was simplified to one automotive segment comprising JLR and Tata Passenger Vehicles plus 'others' (mainly Tata Technologies and Tata Motors Holdings Pte Singapore); prior-period income statements were restated to TMPV only, while prior balance sheets still include CV and are not comparable.
points.quote: The automotive segment will now comprise of JLR and Tata Passenger Vehicles business.

points.point: Capital framing of the standalone PV entity: the India business is net cash, which management said gives flexibility to fund its heavy product investment cycle; one residual link to CV remains — the Rs. 6,500 Cr PLI cap still applies to PV and CV together because the original 2021 application was made as a Group.
points.quote: We had applied originally in 2021 as a Group.

points.point: CV is confirmed out of the reporting perimeter with nothing else changed, and the first demerger cost is booked — a Rs. 400 Cr stamp duty provision within Rs. 1,600 Cr of quarterly exceptionals alongside JLR cyber and India wage-bill charges.
points.quote: Commercial vehicle business is out I think last quarter post the demerger , everything else is the same.

points.point: FY26 exceptionals of about Rs. 4,100 Cr include demerger stamp duty; separately, the two entities now set dividends independently — Rs. 3 per share at TMPV (about Rs. 1,100 Cr outflow) plus Rs. 4 at TMLCV — which management framed as more total distribution than the pre-demerger company paid.
points.quote: So this actually represents a total dividend of Rs. 7 in the year when the demerger was undertaken and an increase over the Rs. 6 that we have paid for the last two years.

verdict.what_management_expects: Stated only indirectly: CV and PV housed in two separate listed entities, each with its own board, leadership and dividend (Rs. 3 + Rs. 4 vs Rs. 6 before); TMPV consolidating PV, EV and JLR under one automotive segment, with a net-cash India business (Rs. 7,000 Cr) giving flexibility to fund its product investment cycle while JLR carries Rs. 33,000 Cr net debt.
verdict.gaps: No value-unlock, focus, valuation or synergy argument; no demerger costs/benefits beyond stamp duty; no dis-synergies, debt-allocation logic, or any investor, lender or partner request.

verdict.rationale: The supplied texts do not contain a rationale for EMBDL separating a business — no demerger, spin-off, scheme of arrangement or business-separation proposal by Embassy Developments Ltd. is described anywhere in them, and the section labelled "SCHEME RATIONALE" is in fact a Regulation 30 intimation about insolvency litigation plus the annexed NCLT order, not a scheme rationale. The only separation referred to is historical and belongs to another group: a court-approved demerger in 2011 under which the power business was separated from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group, after which Sinnar Thermal Power Limited (STPL) has been part of the Ratan India Group. That demerger is mentioned only as background to a liability dispute, not as a value-creation plan: Canara Bank (e-Syndicate Bank) has alleged EMBDL is liable, as purported corporate guarantor, for repayment of Rs. 372 crore (Rs. 3,72,35,67,407.77 as on 30.12.2024, plus penalties and interest from 01.01.2025) of facilities advanced to STPL — original sanctions of Rs. 144.40 crore (Rs. 100.00 crore rupee term loan dated 26.02.2010, Rs. 15.57 crore cost-overrun Term Loan COR-I dated 26.03.2014, Rs. 28.83 crore COR-II dated 30.08.2016) for a 1350 MW (5 x 270) coal-based thermal power project at Sinnar, Nashik — and filed a Section 7 IBC application, which the NCLT Delhi Bench admitted by order dated 09.12.2025 in C.P. (IB) No. 317/ND/2025. Management says the admission "was not warranted on merits," that EMBDL remains financially sound and fully operational with no enforceable obligation for the Borrower's loans, and that it obtained a stay from NCLAT (admitted and stayed on 11.12.2025 per the intimation), with the next hearing noted in the calls as scheduled for 19 (date truncated). verdict.rationale: Note on the premise: in this filing HSCL is not separating out one of its own businesses — it is the Resulting Company receiving a business. The Scheme of Arrangement (Sections 230–232, Companies Act 2013), approved by HSCL's Board on 21 September 2026, demerges the 'Tyre Business of DBRL' from Dalmia Bharat Refractories Limited (Demerged Company) into Himadri Speciality Chemical Ltd (Resulting Company) as a going concern on an 'as is where is' basis, with an Appointed Date of 1 October 2026 (or such other date as the NCLT may approve). The Demerged Undertaking comprises all assets, liabilities, contracts, employees, brands, trademarks, licences, permits, approvals and properties attributable to the Tyre Business, defined as designing, manufacturing and development of all types of tyre and tyre products; its turnover as on 31 March 2026 was INR 149.31 crores, or 3.39% of HSCL's total turnover for FY ended 31 March 2026. The Board's stated reasoning is that, given the nature of the Demerged Undertaking, its future requirements and the respective strengths and strategic objectives of HSCL, the demerger gives the Tyre Business 'more focused ownership and robust operating structure' while letting each company direct management attention, capital and resources to businesses aligned with its own capabilities. For HSCL specifically the filing lists six benefits: forward-integration of the Tyre Business with its existing carbon black and advanced carbon materials business to strengthen its presence across the tyre value chain; leverage of its material expertise, R&D, manufacturing and customer relationships for product customisation and expansion across tyre application segments; operational and commercial synergies in raw material sourcing, product development, manufacturing, logistics, distribution, market development, shared services and customer engagement; direct ownership and control enabling coordinated capacity utilisation, modernisation, product expansion and distribution build-out; greater strategic and financial flexibility to align investment, funding and capacity expansion with group strategy; and long-term growth and value creation for HSCL and its stakeholders. Consideration is non-cash: HSCL will issue 1 new equity share of face value INR 1 for every 260 DBRL shares of face value INR 10, per a 20 September 2026 joint valuation report by SSPA & Co and CA Manish Gadia, with a fairness opinion of the same date from Jajodia Equity Advisors Services Limited. The dilution is minimal — HSCL promoter holding moves from 52.49% to 52.47% and public from 47.51% to 47.53% (total shares 50,45,74,175 to 50,47,50,637, plus 53,896 exercisable ESOPs) — and DBRL's own shareholding pattern (promoter 74.99%, public 25.01%) does not change.
verdict.evolution: The prompt's 'CALL PASSAGES' section is empty — no earnings call transcripts from any year were supplied — so the idea's emergence and evolution across calls cannot be reconstructed from these texts, and nothing here records who asked for it (investors, lenders or partners) or how the plan changed. The only datable sequence in the supplied material is internal to the filing: the joint valuation report and the merchant banker's fairness opinion are both dated 20 September 2026; HSCL's Board approved the Scheme at its meeting on 21 September 2026 and disclosed it to BSE and NSE under Regulation 30 on the same date (Ref. No. HSCL/Stock-Ex/2026-27/59); the Appointed Date is set at 1 October 2026, subject to NCLT; and the sizing is measured against FY ended 31 March 2026. No earlier or alternative version of the plan is described.

points.point: The Board's core rationale is focus and resource allocation: focused ownership and a robust operating structure for the Tyre Business, and each company deploying management attention, capital and resources to businesses matching its own strategic capabilities.

points.point: Benefit (f) and the closing statement frame the Scheme as serving shareholders, employees, creditors and other stakeholders, supporting the Tyre Business's sustainable growth while each company focuses on its own objectives.
points.quote: The proposed Scheme is in the best interest of the respective Companies, their shareholders, employees, creditors and other stakeholders, and is expected to facilitate the sustainable growth of the Demerged Undertaking while enabling each Company to focus on its respective strategic objectives.

points.point: Consideration is share-based, not cash: HSCL issues 1 share of FV INR 1 for every 260 DBRL shares of FV INR 10, based on the 20 September 2026 joint valuation by SSPA & Co and CA Manish Gadia, with a fairness opinion from Jajodia Equity Advisors Services Limited.

points.point: Dilution at HSCL is negligible — promoter 52.49% to 52.47%, public 47.51% to 47.53%, share count 50,45,74,175 to 50,47,50,637 — while DBRL's shareholding pattern is unchanged; HSCL's new shares will be listed on BSE and NSE, where it is already listed.

verdict.rationale: Management framed the demerger as splitting one company that had been doing two businesses with two different investor bases: an asset-heavy business that designs, develops, finances and owns hotels (pension funds, insurance companies betting on inflation, repricing and annuity yield) and an asset-light business that monetises brand, management, loyalty, distribution and technology with almost no capital intensity. Keswani said Lemon Tree had only built hotels in 2004-2007 because owners would not hand their hotels to an unknown brand, and that with the brand now widely recognised (MakeMyTrip's CEO told him 20-25% of occupancy comes from them the moment a Lemon Tree opens) there was no reason to keep owning assets rather than monetise the brand — explicitly the Marriott/Host Hotels and Hilton/Park Hotels playbook. Mechanically (Composite Scheme approved 9 Jan 2026, appointed date 1 April 2026): Carnation Hotels and Hamstede Living merge into LTH; Oriole Dr. Fresh, Canary, Sukhsagar and Manakin merge into Fleur against shares to LTH; and the Demerged Undertaking — 11 operating hotels plus Aurika Shimla under construction, the investment in Arum (Aurika Shillong, 165 rooms) and the entire development capability/team with exclusivity on all future ownership, leasing and development — demerges into Fleur, with 20 Fleur shares for every 311 LTH shares (demerged division turnover Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover; 1,563 operating rooms across 15 hotels per the presentation, 1,820 keys/17 hotels per the press release). A second stated problem was conflict of interest: development capability was moved to Fleur with 'Chinese firewalls' so Fleur shareholders could never feel Lemon Tree was cherry-picking the best assets for itself, and Lemon Tree must refer new acquisition/development opportunities to Fleur. All group debt (about Rs 1,300 crore at demerger, Rs 1,500 crore total borrowings at FY26-end, cost of debt 7.42%) goes to Fleur, leaving Lemon Tree debt-free with only technology and marketing spend, forcing the Board to frame a dividend/shareholder-reward policy. Warburg Pincus (Coastal Cedar Investments B.V.) bought APG's entire 41.09% of Fleur and committed up to Rs 960 crore of primary equity, giving Fleur roughly Rs 3,000 crore of deployable capital at 1:1 debt-equity against 2,500+ rooms under active discussion and Aurika Nehru Place (572 rooms, ~Rs 700 crore); post-scheme LTH shareholders own ~74% of Fleur (32.96% direct plus ~41% through LTH) versus the 59% LTH owns today, and Fleur lists separately for 'transparent price discovery and market-driven valuation of the asset-heavy business'.
verdict.evolution: The idea was first visible as a Fleur listing aspiration in the Nov 2024 call, where Keswani said debt-freedom would come sooner 'if we list Fleur before that' and put an IPO 'within the next 2-3 years at most'; in the Aug 2025 call he disclosed that committees of directors had been set up in both Lemon Tree and Fleur to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via a demerger and listing it, alongside splitting the management teams (Neelendra Singh for LTH from 1 October, Saurabh Shatdal for Fleur), with listing hoped for end-CY2026. In the Nov 2025 call it was 'in process' with a Board subcommittee and a promise of 'some other even more exciting stuff' within three months; the scheme, the Warburg/APG transactions and the 74%/26% shareholding math were announced in the Jan 2026 (15 January) dedicated call with a 12-15 month path to listing. By the Feb 2026 call Keswani confirmed the scheme was effective from 1 April and, responding to Ashish Kumar's request, promised pro forma financials for both entities; those pro formas appeared with the Jun 2026 (29 May) results, where CCI approval (April 2026), Warburg's completed purchase of APG's stake and a longer 12-18 month NCLT-dependent timeline were given, followed by NSE/BSE observation letters on 22 September 2026.

points.point: Asked directly by Kunal Lakhan (CLSA) what was wrong with the old structure, Keswani said the hotel business has two subsets with two different investor types — developers/owners wanting chunky yield and inflation-linked annuity returns versus asset-light investors betting on brand and management — and Lemon Tree was a combination of both.
points.quote: We have actually separated 2 types of businesses. One is asset heavy, long -term appreciating asset, capital intensive. It has a different kind of investor, and this business has a very different kind of investor, and we wanted to actually attract both types of investors.

points.point: He explained the historical accident being corrected: hotels were built only to establish the brand, and with the brand now established the company should monetise it instead of owning assets.
points.quote: We were forced to build hotels to build our brand. But once we build our brand, technically, we do not need hotels because now it is time for Lemon Tree to monetize its brand, which is enormous recall.

points.point: The transfer of the development capability and exclusive development mandate to Fleur was driven by a conflict-of-interest problem — Fleur minorities fearing Lemon Tree would keep the best projects for itself — and was solved with firewalls.
points.quote: Development capability was an issue which was raised in order to maximize Fleur's growth, we did not want shareholders of Fleur to ever feel that Lemon Tree when it recommends any assets was cherry -picking, which means Lemon Tree would say, I have got this very nice asset in Delhi, why should I offer it to Fleur.

points.point: All of Lemon Tree's debt moves to Fleur: Fleur carries roughly Rs 1,300 crore of debt against a ~Rs 900 crore net EBITDA and can borrow another ~Rs 1,300 crore, while Lemon Tree goes to zero debt.
points.quote: Firstly, when this demerger happens, all the debt, including the Lemon Tree's debt, after adjustment is being transferred to Fleur. Fleur will have 100% of our debt and Lemon Tree will have zero debt.

points.point: Keswani justified keeping a ~41% indirect stake in Fleur (challenged by Jinesh Joshi on hold-co discount) as Lemon Tree retaining 'skin in the game' as Fleur's manager, with natural dilution as Fleur raises capital; he quantified that Rs 1,000 crore deployed by Fleur generates ~Rs 350 crore of turnover, Rs 170-180 crore EBITDA and ~Rs 30 crore of fees for Lemon Tree.
points.quote: We felt it was prudent to have significant skin in the game at this stage, which means that going forward, it is very possible that Lemon Tree may dilute or even increase its stake over time; this will obviously be a Board decision .

points.point: Warburg's Rs 960 crore primary commitment plus Fleur's own cash and 1:1 debt gives roughly Rs 3,000 crore to deploy pre-listing against 2,500 rooms in active discussion; Keswani guided Fleur to over Rs 1,000 crore net EBITDA by FY28 and Lemon Tree to 80% EBITDA margin / 60% PAT margin.
points.quote: We have potentially about Rs 3,000 crores available to deploy in this growth before we list.

points.point: Opening the call with pro forma financials for both entities, Keswani described the transaction as simple — Warburg has bought APG's Fleur stake, Lemon Tree transfers 17 hotels and development capabilities in exchange for Fleur shares to LTH shareholders, and Fleur lists.
points.quote: This scheme will result in 2 distinct financially sound businesses.

points.point: He restated the economic outcome for each entity: Lemon Tree debt-free, high-margin, high-ROCE and fee/brand-driven; Fleur the consolidated owner of a fully renovated portfolio, post-scheme India's largest hotel platform by inventory at 5,600 rooms and 39 operational hotels.
points.quote: Post the reorganization , Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt -free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand -related income.

points.point: Shareholder arithmetic: LTH shareholders end up with close to 74% of Fleur (33% direct, ~41% through Lemon Tree) versus the 59% Lemon Tree directly owns in Fleur today, before Warburg's primary infusion; Keswani also said he will cease to be executive at Lemon Tree from March 2027 and focus on Fleur as Executive Chair.
points.quote: Post reorganization , Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own close to 74% of Fleur Hotels, 33% directly and about 41% indirectly through Lemon Tree.

points.point: Answering Achal Kumar, Keswani confirmed Fleur will be brand-agnostic post-demerger and may hand assets to other operators — Lemon Tree has no automatic right to Fleur's hotels and must earn them on results.
points.quote: Yes. But Lemon Tree must be able to deliver best results to get it . Just because Lemon Tree has skin in the game with Fleur does not mean that it has an automatic right to any asset that Fleur develops.

points.point: On capital allocation after the split, Lemon Tree is expected to need almost no capital and move to distributing profits, while Fleur will retain capital for growth rather than pay dividends.
points.quote: Lemon Tree will not need any significant capital other than potentially investments in technology or in marketing and so on. It will be essentially a zero -debt cash accretive company.

points.point: Keswani confirmed the scheme is effective from 1 April and that Lemon Tree becomes debt-free from next year, with all assets and debt going to Fleur and fee income becoming free cash; the Board must decide a dividend policy within six months.
points.quote: What will happen is in the scheme of demerger, all the assets of Lemon Tree, including its debt will be transferred to Fleur. Lemon Tree will immediately effectively be a debt -free company from next year.

points.point: Investors pushed for separate reporting: Ashish Kumar of Infinity Alternatives asked for pro forma financials of both businesses while awaiting the listing, and management agreed to publish them from the next quarter.
points.quote: Now that we have decided on the split of the 2 businesses, what might be helpful is if we can add pro forma financials for both of the assets as they look like so that while we are waiting for the l isting, we do get a good sense of what the numbers are looking like.

points.point: Keswani positioned the asset-light entity as a first in India, with fee income from hotels signed three years earlier only now flowing, and Fleur guided to ~Rs 1,000 crore EBITDA by FY28, its first year as a listed company.
points.quote: And keep in mind that Lemon Tree will be the first fully asset -light brand owning tech and distribution and management company in India, the first.

points.point: The demerger was still with Board subcommittees of both Lemon Tree and Fleur, with management hinting that more than the demerger was being negotiated (the Warburg/APG transactions announced two months later).
points.quote: It is not only the demerger of Fleur, but some other even more exciting stuff, but we will talk about it when the time is right.

points.point: First formal disclosure of the structure: committees of directors in both companies to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via demerger and then list Fleur, with Lemon Tree becoming asset-light and focused on management, brand and technology — described as the global trend in the space.
points.quote: You may have also seen that we have said that a committee of directors has been set up in Lemon Tree and in Fleur to evaluate how we can possibly look at a transfer of assets from Lemon Tree into Fleur through a demerger scheme and then automatically look at how we can list Fleur.

points.point: The separation of management was done first and explicitly for this purpose — Neelendra Singh to run asset-light Lemon Tree from 1 October and Saurabh Shatdal to drive Fleur's asset-heavy growth, with Keswani handholding and moving to strategic oversight.
points.quote: The intent of the leadership change was to get 2 very good people who would then run these two companies independently on a day -to-day basis.

points.point: Keswani drew a hard line on mandates — Fleur builds, buys and leases, Lemon Tree only manages or franchises — and noted that the more Fleur dilutes and raises capital, the more Lemon Tree's economic interest rises via fees (Rs 100+ crore this year, potentially Rs 300-400 crore from Fleur in three years).
points.quote: Fleur's mandate will be to focus on, at the right value, building, buying, or leasing hotels. Lemon Tree's will only be to manage or franchise. Lemon Tree will not lease hotels once the Fleur demerger happens.

points.point: The earliest trace in these calls: a Fleur listing was already seen as the accelerator of deleveraging, with Keswani putting an IPO within 2-3 years at most when asked by Prashant Biyani.
points.quote: I think we are sticking to our guidance that in the next 3 - 3.5 years, we should be debt free , but if we list Fleur before that then we will be debt free that much earlier.

points.point: The 9 Jan 2026 filing states the Board reviewed the business with a view to segregating the asset-heavy ownership/development undertaking from the asset-light management/brand platform, and that the demerged business is self-sustaining and better housed in Fleur; the demerged division's turnover was Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover.
points.quote: Therefore, to achieve operational focus, greater flexibility for capital deployment, and clearer alignment of business objectives, it is proposed under this Scheme to (i) amalgamate Transferor Company 3, Transferor Company 4, Transferor Company 5 and Transferor Company 6 with the Transferee Company; and (ii) demerge and vest the Demerged Undertaking (comprising the Demerged Hotel Properties and the Development Capabilities together with the related undertakings, as defined hereinafter) into the Transferee C ompany, while the Company will continue to focus on the asset -light hotel management support, brand and operations including management support of the hotels transferred to the Transferee Company and other properties.

points.point: A stated purpose is market-driven valuation: Fleur ceases to be LTH's subsidiary and lists, so LTH shareholders participate directly in the asset-heavy business through listed shares rather than through a subsidiary.
points.quote: Following the implementation of the Scheme, the Transferee Company will cease to be a subsidiary of the Company , and its shares will be listed on the Stock Exchanges, enabling transparent price discovery and market -driven valuation of the asset -heavy business.

points.point: The filing also sets out structural clean-up and partner-flexibility objectives: merging two wholly owned subsidiaries into LTH to remove layering and cost, and creating a structure that lets Fleur bring in investors or co-development partners per project without touching LTH's brand operations.

verdict.rationale: The texts supplied do not support the premise of a separation: the only substantive document here is a scheme of AMALGAMATION (consolidation), not a demerger or spin-off, and no earnings-call passages were included in the prompt at all — the "CALL PASSAGES" section is empty. What the filing establishes is that Dr. Agarwal's Eye Hospital Limited ("AEHL", the Transferor Company, the listed legacy entity) is to be merged into Dr. Agarwal's Health Care Limited ("AHCL", the Transferee Company) under Section 2(1B) of the Income-tax Act and Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013, with AEHL's undertaking vesting in AHCL as a going concern and AEHL standing dissolved without being wound up. Consideration is 23 AHCL shares for every 2 AEHL shares, recommended in a Valuation Report supported by Fairness Opinions; AHCL's own existing holding in AEHL is cancelled, collapsing the cross-holding between the two listed Agarwal entities. AEHL's authorised capital of 2,00,00,000 shares of INR 10 each is reclassified into 20,00,00,000 shares of INR 1 each and transferred to AHCL's authorised capital, and AHCL-granted options held by AEHL employees carry on unchanged — mechanics consistent with folding a subsidiary-cum-listed-affiliate into the parent platform. The Appointed Date is the opening of business on April 01, 2026. Critically, the filing itself states that the commercial rationale sits in the Section 232(2)(c) board reports at Annexure VA and VB, which are NOT in the text provided — so the actual "why" (business overlap, related-party and two-listed-vehicle governance issues, cost or tax synergies, whatever management argued) cannot be reconstructed from these passages. Governance signals are visible but are not reasons: every Agarwal family director (Dr. Amar, Dr. Athiya, Dr. Adil, Dr. Anosh) recused as an Interested Director under Section 184(2), and Mr. Venkatraman Balakrishnan recused at AHCL as a Common Independent Director of both companies — pointing to a promoter-affiliated related-party transaction, with Ranjan Ramdas Pai, Sanjay Dharambir Anand, Nachiket Mor and Archana Jayaraman Bhaskar voting in favour.

verdict.rationale: The texts provided do not describe a separation, spin-off or demerger at all, and no earnings-call passages were supplied — the CALL PASSAGES section is empty, so nothing can be attributed to management commentary. What the filing text describes is the opposite transaction: a Scheme of Amalgamation in which Cigniti Technologies Limited (the Transferor Company, a digital assurance and engineering / software-testing business using AI-driven Continuous Testing and Test Automation, listed on BSE and NSE) is merged into Coforge Limited (the Transferee Company, an IT and IT-enabled services provider across financial services, insurance, travel, transportation and logistics, manufacturing and distribution, and government). The commercial backdrop given is that Coforge had already bought control before the scheme: by 27 December 2024 it held 54% of Cigniti's expanded share capital, having acquired 72,35,865 equity shares between October and December 2024 for approximately INR 10,239 million, and both boards approved the original scheme that same day, 27 December 2024. Consideration was set by a Joint Valuation Report of PwC Business Consulting Services LLP and KPMG Valuation Services LLP at a share exchange ratio of 1:5 (one INR 10 Coforge share for five INR 10 Cigniti shares), with fairness opinions from JM Financial Limited and Axis Capital Limited. That ratio was later restated to 1:1 by a Joint Clarification Note dated 13 June 2025 purely because Coforge split each INR 10 share into five INR 2 shares (board 04 March 2025, shareholders 17 April 2025, record date 04 June 2025); the filing stresses the revised ratio is "mathematically and economically equivalent" to the original and conveys no substantive change in value, with Axis (16 June 2025) and JM Financial (19 June 2025) reconfirming fairness, and both boards approving the amended scheme on 06 July 2025. Critically, the extract itself does not reproduce the rationale: it states the rationale "ha[s] been set out in detail in the First Motion Order dated 17 October 2025" and is only "briefly recapitulated herein", and the recapitulation that follows is procedural — incorporation history, registered-office shifts to Gurugram, share capital, exchange ratio, exchange and tribunal steps — with no stated synergy, margin, capital, focus or valuation reasoning. No investor, lender or partner is identified as having asked for the transaction; stakeholders simply voted in favour, and no objections were received from any shareholder or creditor.
verdict.evolution: No earnings calls were provided, so there is no call-by-call evolution and no call dates to cite. The only sequence available is from the filing: board approval of the original scheme plus the 1:5 valuation and fairness opinions on 27 December 2024, after Coforge's October–December 2024 purchase of 54% of Cigniti; the Coforge stock split (board 04 March 2025, shareholders 17 April 2025, record date 04 June 2025) prompting the 13 June 2025 restatement of the ratio to 1:1 and amended board approvals on 06 July 2025; then NSE and BSE observation letters on 17 and 18 July 2025, the First Motion Order of 17 October 2025, stakeholder meetings on 06 December 2025, Chairperson's Reports of 08 December 2025, the Second Motion petition filed 15 December 2025, and admission by the Tribunal on 09 January 2026. That is a change in transaction mechanics and process, not a change in a separation plan.

verdict.rationale: The documents do not describe a separation: the only corporate action in these texts is the opposite — an amalgamation in which Happiest Minds Technologies Ltd (Transferor) is absorbed into ITC Infotech India Ltd (Transferee) and then dissolved without being wound up, under definitive agreements and a Merger Framework Agreement dated August 31, 2026 among Happiest Minds, ITC Infotech, Mr Ashok Soota and Ashok Soota Medical Research LLP. Management's stated reasoning is complementarity and scale: Happiest Minds' AI, digital engineering, cloud, data, analytics and cybersecurity capabilities combined with ITC Infotech's enterprise transformation, SAP, PLM, cloud, Industry 4.0 and industry-specific solutions, to create 'a scaled, AI First Global Technology Services Enterprise' targeting US$1 billion of annual revenue by FY28, with 19,000+ employees, 800+ customers and operations in 30+ countries. The scheme rationale lists: a single globally credible platform from combined capabilities, customer relationships and talent pools; greater synergies via shared financial, managerial, technical and marketing resources; increased scale, focus, cross-selling to a larger customer base, productivity and operational efficiencies, stronger partner-ecosystem relationships and augmented intellectual capital; wider professional opportunities and better employee retention; and an enhanced competitive position in domestic and global markets. Two explicitly financial motives are named: greater efficiency in cash management with 'unfettered access' to combined cash flows for funding growth, and augmentation of the Transferee's ability to raise equity and debt capital. Consideration is share-based — 25 ITC Infotech shares of INR 10 each for every 81 Happiest Minds shares of INR 2 each (other than those held by ITC Infotech itself), based on a joint valuation report of August 31, 2026 by PwC Business Consulting Services LLP and GT Valuation Advisors, with a fairness opinion of the same date from ICICI Securities; ITC Infotech's shares are to be listed by virtue of the scheme, and ITC Infotech separately acquires an aggregate minority stake (amount truncated in the text supplied). Happiest Minds' pre-scheme shareholding as on August 31, 2026 was 6,73,23,400 promoter shares (44.21%) and 8,49,51,411 non-promoter shares (55.79%) of 15,22,74,811 total. The only 'carve-out' discussed on the calls is a measurement exercise, not a business separation: management said AI is spread across the company rather than sitting inside the GBS bucket, so they would go project by project across the whole revenue stream and carve out AI-led revenue — not by technology but by the impact or relevance of AI — to disclose what portion of the quarter's INR 625 crores is AI-led, with the exercise to be completed by end-September and reported at the end of Q2. The texts name no investor, lender or partner as having asked for the transaction.
verdict.evolution: Only one call passage is supplied (Jul 2026), and it contains no reference to any merger, demerger or separation of a business — it addresses only how AI-led revenue will be identified and reported, citing SecAIGenie in security as AI work sitting outside GBS, and committing to a carved-out AI-led revenue number by end-September/end-Q2. The corporate action appears for the first time in the August 31, 2026 filings: the press release announcing the ITC Infotech combination, the Merger Framework Agreement of the same date, and the scheme rationale. So on this evidence the idea cannot be traced call by call; there is no three-year arc in the passages given, and no earlier-call foreshadowing to compare against the final structure.

verdict.rationale: The texts provided do not contain any separation, demerger, spin-off or scheme-of-arrangement rationale, so no reasoning for a business separation can be reconstructed from them. The 'CALL PASSAGES' section is empty — no earnings call transcript passages were supplied for any of the three years, so there is no management commentary to draw on. What is labelled 'SCHEME RATIONALE' is not a scheme rationale: it is a set of SEBI LODR Regulation 30 stock-exchange intimations about insolvency proceedings. The first (Ref: JPVL:SEC:2026, 17th March 2026, with the parallel JAL:SEC:2026 disclosure) reports that the NCLT Allahabad Bench orally pronounced an order under Section 31 of the IBC approving the resolution plan dated October 14, 2025 submitted by Adani Enterprises Limited for Jaiprakash Associates Limited, the promoter company of JPVL — under which JAL's securities will be delisted, the liquidation value is stated to be insufficient to satisfy secured creditors in full, NIL consideration is offered to JAL shareholders, and JAL's pre-CIRP share capital is to be cancelled and extinguished for zero consideration by an Effective Date no later than 90 days from NCLT approval. The second (Ref: JPVL:SEC:2026, 27th February 2026) reports that NARCL, through India Debt Resolution Company Limited, filed a Section 7 IBC application before the NCLT Allahabad Bench at Prayagraj to initiate CIRP against JPVL itself, alleging default of Rs. 511,72,82,207 plus interest and charges on a corporate guarantee JPVL extended to Jaiprakash Associates Limited, a matter also under dispute before DRT-III, Delhi. These are promoter-insolvency and corporate-guarantee-liability disclosures, not a separation of any JPVL business, and they name no businesses being separated, no transferor or resulting entity, no share entitlement ratio, no appointed date, and no stated benefits. Answering the question as posed would require inventing facts not present in the supplied texts, which was explicitly ruled out.

verdict.rationale: The materials supplied do not contain any statement of why Laurus Labs Ltd. is separating a business: the "CALL PASSAGES" section is empty (no earnings-call text was included), and the three documents filed under "SCHEME RATIONALE" are purely procedural Regulation 30 disclosure letters, not the scheme's rationale section, which is described as "truncated" and in fact contains none of it. What the documents do establish is the structure of the transaction: a Composite Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013 among Laurus Synthesis Private Limited (LSPL, the Demerged/Transferor Company), Sriam Labs Private Limited (Sriam, the Resulting Company) — both wholly-owned subsidiaries of Laurus Labs — and Laurus Labs Limited (Transferee Company). The scheme has two legs: (i) the "Identified Business Undertaking," i.e. Unit-1 of LSPL, is demerged into Sriam Labs; and (ii) the "Remaining Business Undertakings" of LSPL (entire LSPL excluding Unit-1) are amalgamated into Laurus Labs Limited itself. Because both entities are already wholly-owned subsidiaries, this is an internal reorganisation of subsidiary assets rather than a listed-shareholder spin-off, and no share-entitlement ratio, valuation, financials or segment numbers appear in the texts. Procedurally, unsecured creditors of both LSPL and Sriam approved the scheme at NCLT-directed meetings held April 06, 2026 with requisite quorum; the NCLT Amravati Special Branch passed an order on July 24, 2026 directing service of Form CAA-3 notices on authorities, regulators and stakeholders, and set the petition hearing for September 10, 2026. No business reason, no cited metric, no named investor, lender or partner request, and no mention of margins, capital allocation or value unlocking appears anywhere in the supplied material. Any rationale beyond the structural facts above cannot be reconstructed from these texts, and I am not supplying one from memory.
verdict.evolution: Only the filing trail is visible, and it is procedural rather than substantive: the July 25, 2026 letter back-references prior scheme disclosures dated August 21, 2025 and September 05, 2025 (first disclosures), then February 24, 2026 (NCLT direction to convene unsecured-creditor meetings), then April 07, 2026 (creditors of both LSPL and Sriam approved the scheme at meetings held April 06, 2026). On July 25, 2026 the company disclosed the NCLT order pronounced July 24, 2026 directing CAA-3 notices and fixing September 10, 2026 as the next hearing; as of today no outcome of that hearing is in the supplied documents. A further letter dated October 6, 2026 concerns an unrelated INR 12,09,60,500 rights-issue investment in associate Kurnool Renewables Private Limited (holding unchanged at 26%), not the scheme. There are no earnings calls in the input, so no call-by-call evolution of the idea can be traced.

verdict.rationale: The supplied texts do not contain management's stated reasoning — the only document provided is the NSE observation letter (Ref: NSE/LIST/52937, May 15, 2026) and the opening of the BSE letter (DCS/AMAL/RD/R37/73/2026-27), both procedural, and the 'CALL PASSAGES' section of the prompt is empty. What the filing does establish is structure, not motive: this is a Composite Scheme of Arrangement under sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 between Lloyds Realty Developers Limited ('Transferor Company 1'), Indrajit Properties Private Limited ('Transferor Company 2'), Lloyds Enterprises Limited ('LEL' or 'Transferee Company') and Lloyds Realty Limited ('Resulting Company'), filed under Regulation 37 of SEBI LODR read with the SEBI Master Circular of June 20, 2023. So two private/unlisted entities are absorbed into listed LEL while a resulting company, Lloyds Realty Limited, is created and taken to listing — implying a realty business is being carved out of LEL into a separately listed vehicle, with shares allotted to LEL shareholders per a share exchange ratio. The exchange explicitly left the rationale to be supplied by the company later, directing LEL to put before shareholders the 'Need for the merger/demerger, rationale of the scheme and swap ratio, synergies of business of the entities involved in the scheme, impact of the scheme on the minority shareholders and cost benefit analysis of the scheme,' plus the valuation report, growth-rate justification, and three years of Revenue, PAT and EBITDA for every entity. Lenders feature only as a consent gate, not as requesters: NOCs are required from lending scheduled commercial banks/financial institutions/debenture trustees per para A(2)(k) of Part-I of the SEBI Master Circular, and any 'Conditions imposed by lenders' must be disclosed with their impact on the scheme. SEBI's own comment of May 15, 2026 requires disclosure of all ongoing adjudication, recovery and enforcement proceedings against the company, its promoters and directors before the NCLT and shareholders. No numbers, margins, segment figures, investor requests or partner demands appear anywhere in the provided text, so any specific rationale would have to be invented — which I will not do.
verdict.evolution: No earnings-call passages were supplied — the 'CALL PASSAGES:' heading in the prompt is followed by nothing, so there is no call-by-call record to trace and no call dates to cite. The only dated evidence is regulatory and terminal rather than formative: the NSE observation letter and SEBI's comments, both dated May 15, 2026, with the no-objection valid for six months from that date within which the scheme must be filed with the NCLT. By that point the structure was already fixed in the draft scheme, and NSE barred further change — 'no changes to the draft scheme except those mandated by the regulators/ authorities / tribunals shall be made without specific written consent of SEBI' — so nothing in these texts shows how or when the idea surfaced or how it was revised.
